headings.text: ADR-048 — RelayTransport: direct-vs-relay endpoint fallback policy

html:
#ADR-048 — RelayTransport: direct-vs-relay endpoint fallback policy

#Status

Accepted. Three designs were proposed, red-teamed, revised, and proven with real compiled, sanitized, and benchmarked C++ (MSVC 19.51 + clang++ 22.1, ASan/UBSan; TSan unavailable on this MSVC-ABI toolchain, substituted per VERIFICATION.md's Windows exclusion policy with reentrancy asserts + ASan+UBSan + run-to-run determinism checks). One design is disqualified by a proven correctness violation of a MUST invariant. Of the two safe survivors, Design 2 — DirectThenRelay<TimeoutMs>, the wall-clock fallback-threshold policy — is selected.

#Question

Today TcpTransport (include/quark/net/tcp_transport.hpp) requires a direct TCP path to every peer: add_peer(Endpoint) teaches it one NodeId → Endpoint mapping, and a peer with no reachable listener (behind NAT / a restrictive firewall) simply cannot be dialed — send_on_loop drops the frame (010 dead-letter) if no endpoint resolves, and even when an endpoint is known, a connect that never succeeds cycles forever through St::Backoff with jittered exponential retry (tcp_transport.hpp:61-62, 207-235) — there is no terminal "direct is unreachable" signal anywhere in the existing state machine.

Quark needs a third way for two nodes to exchange frames when neither can dial the other directly: routing through an intermediary relay node's already-open connections to both, TURN-style. The architecture is settled and was not re-litigated here (see prior discussion, retained below); the only open crux this ADR settles is the fallback-threshold policy — given that direct-connect failure has no terminal signal (just endless Backoff), what threshold decides "give up on direct, dial the relay endpoint instead," how is that threshold expressed as a CRTP-style policy parameter (matching Sequential / Priority<P> / Placement<...> / DrainBudget<N>, policies.hpp), and what re-probing behavior (if any) recovers a peer back to direct once its NAT/firewall state changes — without reordering or duplicating that peer's frames.

Settled architecture (not re-litigated):

  • Client side: no new Transport implementation — a policy that resolves, per peer, which Endpoint to dial (the peer's own listener vs. a designated relay node's listener). Still plain TcpTransport underneath, reusing its existing dedup/backoff/framing machinery unchanged.
  • Relay side: a thin forwarding hook on on_receive() — "if frame.to != self, send(frame.to, frame) instead of delivering locally" — decorator-shaped like SecureTransport (include/quark/core/secure_transport.hpp), not a parallel transport hierarchy. MessageFrame already carries to: NodeId (transport.hpp:61-74).

#Designs (one-line summaries)

  1. Count-based threshold — DirectThenRelay<MaxAttempts>. Falls back after MaxAttempts consecutive Backoff cycles; a successful Open resets the counter. Revised to inject the policy at runtime via configure_relay_fallback<P>() (function-pointer extraction) rather than templating TcpTransport itself, and to replace a single global recovery watermark with a per-peer "chasing" watermark (relay_enqueued/relay_drained) that re-arms on every new send admitted through the still-open relay gate.
  2. Time-based threshold — DirectThenRelay<TimeoutMs>. Falls back once TimeoutMs has elapsed since the peer's first St::Connecting with no Open in between — a one-shot io_.post_after timer is the authoritative backstop (Backoff re-entry is only an opportunistic early check), which is what catches a black-holed connect() that never errors out of Connecting at all. Recovery uses an out-of-band probe connection that proves direct reachability before a fenced, never-mid-frame cutover swaps the live Conn's fd in place. TcpTransport itself is not templated — the policy tag resolves to one runtime int64_t field at construction, and relay configuration is two ordinary runtime calls (set_relay, an optional timeout constructor parameter).
  3. Hybrid attempt/time-capped threshold with throttled recovery — DirectThenRelay<MaxAttempts, TimeoutMs, RecheckIntervalMs>. Relay kicks in at whichever bound fires first; recovery reuses the same Backoff/reconnect loop at a throttled cadence (no second connection lifecycle), and a Draining sub-state (gated by a per-peer out_peer-aware barrier that also inspects the relay Conn's own in-flight output buffer, not just the not-yet-started queue) defers the direct cutover until every relay-hop frame — including one physically mid-send — has left the wire. TcpTransport is templated on the policy (TcpTransport<FallbackPolicy>), requiring a mechanical TcpTransport<> migration at four existing bare-member-declaration call sites (samples/15_tcp_cluster, samples/17_tcp_cluster_mesh, samples/20_swim_membership_ stability, tests/tcp_distribution_integration_test.cpp).

#Non-goals (deferred to follow-on ADRs)

  • Relay-hop backpressure semantics (hop-local vs. end-to-end congestion signalling through the relay).
  • Relay-node discovery/advertisement mechanism (static config vs. SWIM capability gossip, ADR-045).
  • Multi-relay / relay failover (what happens when the chosen relay node itself goes down).
  • Security posture of the relay node itself (routing-metadata trust boundary; relay authentication beyond ordinary peer mTLS, ADR-040).

#Cross-examination summary

All three designs were red-teamed against the real tcp_transport.hpp/pal/ source (not just their own pseudocode). Every design conceded at least one fatal or serious finding and revised:

  • Design 1 conceded a fatal reordering hole in its original global recovery-watermark barrier, and a fatal outq_ re-keying regression that broke close_peer's SWIM-death dead-letter contract and turned one relay-connection failure into collateral loss for every co-routed peer. Both were redesigned (per-peer chasing watermark; tagged QueuedFrame{to,bytes} entries) before proving.
  • Design 2 conceded two fatal integration gaps against the real source: do_reconnect() was never actually wired to the relay-endpoint resolver (verified by reading tcp_transport.hpp:576- 608 directly — the original claim that this was "one indirection function" already patched in was false), so relay-routing silently and permanently reverted to a broken direct dial the first time the relay leg itself needed any ordinary reconnect; and cutover_to_direct re-registered an already-registered fd via add_fd without a preceding del_fd, which fails silently (EEXIST) on the real Linux/epoll pal backend (confirmed at pal/linux_x86_64/net.hpp:305-312), muting the recovered connection and busy-spinning the shared io_ thread. Both were fixed (resolve_dial_ endpoint() wired into both dial()/ensure_conn() and do_reconnect(); del_fd before add_fd in cutover_to_direct) and re-proven.
  • Design 3 conceded the same class-template/CTAD compile break at four real call sites, a fatal local reordering gap (the drain-before-cutover barrier only checked outq_, never the relay Conn's own partially-sent out buffer), and a fatal salvage_out mis-filing bug once a relay Conn multiplexes several logical peers (c->peer is the relay's id, not the frame's destination, so a torn frame was silently, permanently orphaned). All three were fixed (TcpTransport<> migration disclosed; out_peer-aware barrier; out_peer-keyed salvage_out) and re-proven.

#Evidence table

Totals: 21 claims survived red-team and were proven CORRECT; 1 claim (Design 1's C2r) survived red-team as revised but was proven WRONG against a MUST invariant, with no fix implemented or re-proven.

#Decision

Winner: Design 2 — DirectThenRelay<TimeoutMs>, the wall-clock fallback-threshold policy for TcpTransport, with the fd-handoff and dial-target-resolution fixes applied.

Design 1 is disqualified under the safety/correctness gate. C2r — "in-flight frames are not reordered across a mid-flight relay→direct recovery" — is exactly one of this ADR's MUST invariants ("If the design ever transitions a peer from relay back to direct mid-flight, in-flight frames must not be reordered or duplicated relative to peer FIFO, 017-Delivery-Guarantees"). It was proven WRONG with a reproducible 50–57% inversion rate, not a rare race: any frame enqueued for a peer in the window between the fallback threshold firing and the relay route actually taking effect is queued to the direct hop (because route_hop is evaluated once, at enqueue time, against the not-yet-flipped relay_routed flag) and can arrive after dozens of subsequently, correctly relay-routed frames. The prover identified the root cause (no migration of already-queued direct-hop frames on a fallback flip) but no fix was designed, implemented, or re-proven within this round. Per the judging rubric, a proven-WRONG correct-class claim disqualifies the design from winning unless a stated and proven cheap fix exists — none does here, so Design 1 does not win regardless of its other 7 correct proofs (including the genuinely strong F3 multi-peer contention measurement no other design produced).

Designs 2 and 3 both fully survived: every claim proven CORRECT, zero WRONG verdicts, real ASan (+UBSan via clang) clean across all concurrency stress runs, TSan's absence handled per this project's documented Windows/MSVC sanitizer-exclusion policy (reentrancy asserts + real clang ASan+UBSan + cross-run determinism as the substitute, matching VERIFICATION.md's stated posture for this toolchain). Between them:

  1. Architectural fit. Design 2 keeps TcpTransport exactly the class it is today — no template parameter, zero existing call sites touched. Relay behavior is injected via one optional constructor argument (a policy tag resolved once to a plain int64_t field, DrainBudget<N>- style) plus an ordinary runtime set_relay() call, marshaled through the same started_-gated io_.post() idiom add_peer() already uses. This is the most literal realization of this ADR's own settled premise — "still plain TcpTransport underneath" — of the three designs. Design 3 templates TcpTransport<FallbackPolicy> and, even with CTAD covering constructor call sites, requires a disclosed, mechanical edit to 4 existing files (samples/15_tcp_cluster, samples/ 17_tcp_cluster_mesh, samples/20_swim_membership_stability, tests/tcp_distribution_integration_ test.cpp) that otherwise fail to compile. A bigger, unforced footprint change is a reason to prefer the alternative when both are otherwise proven equally safe and correct (rubric rule 4).
  2. Hot-path evidence quality. Design 3's F1 evidence is genuinely the stronger artifact — it runs the project's own real, unmodified bench/mailbox_bench.cpp (the actual 023 budget-gate instrument) rather than a hand-built analog, and its numbers (96.9–100.0 vs 97.5–99.8 M msg/s/core, bit-identical latency percentiles) are the cleanest zero-overhead demonstration produced by any design in this round. Design 2's F1 instead relies on a custom smoke test plus dumpbin disassembly (also conclusive, but a less direct proxy for the actual mailbox/dispatch gate). Weighed against point 1, this does not overturn the decision — the F1 zero-overhead property is binary (either the hot path calls fallback code, or it doesn't; both designs prove it doesn't) — but it is recorded here as a residual quality gap in Design 2's own proof artifacts, not a correctness gap in the design.
  3. Direct-connect-hang coverage. Design 2's give-up decision is a one-shot io_.post_after timer armed at first Connecting, independent of whether Backoff is ever re-entered — this is what catches a black-holed connect() that never errors out of Connecting at all (Design 2's C3, proven: relay-leg churn does not cause the peer's own dead-letter regression). Design 3's MaxAttempts- or-TimeoutMs hybrid also has a timeout backstop and is not worse here, but Design 2's threshold is the simpler, single-purpose mechanism for exactly the "no terminal signal" problem this ADR opened with.

Both are viable, fully-proven implementations; Design 2 is chosen as the one that most faithfully keeps to the settled "no new Transport subclass, plain TcpTransport underneath" architecture with the smallest source-compatibility footprint, while matching Design 3 claim-for-claim on proven safety and correctness.

#What is actually adopted

  • include/quark/net/tcp_transport.hpp gains: an optional fallback_timeout_ns constructor parameter (default 0 = feature off, byte-identical to today); void set_relay(NodeId, Endpoint) marshaled through the existing started_-gated io_.post() idiom; per-Conn fields first_connecting_ns, fallback_epoch; a relay_routed_ set; a probes_ map for out-of-band recovery probing; resolve_dial_endpoint() as the sole dial-target lookup, wired into both ensure_conn()/dial() and do_reconnect() (the fix for the confirmed relay-leg-churn wedge); check_relay_timeout() as the one-shot give-up backstop; cutover_to_direct() with io_.del_fd() called before io_.add_fd() on the recovered fd (the fix for the confirmed silent-mute/busy-spin bug on the real epoll pal backend).
  • include/quark/net/fallback_policy.hpp (new): NoRelayFallback (default, zero-cost) and DirectThenRelay<TimeoutMs> compile-time tags, resolved once at construction to a runtime int64_t, matching the DrainBudget<N>-style "compile-time tag → resolved runtime field with zero cost when unused" idiom already used elsewhere in policies.hpp.
  • No existing call site changes required — net::TcpTransport transport; (bare member declarations, constructor-initializer forms, all of it) continues to compile unchanged across the full sample/ test corpus.

#Residual risks

  • C1's underlying Linux/epoll EEXIST-on-double-add_fd mechanism was not directly reproduced on this box. This dev environment has only the Windows/WSAPoll pal backend available (pal/ windows_x86_64/net.hpp's add_fd unconditionally overwrites handlers_[fd], masking the bug class entirely), so the fix (del_fd before add_fd) is verified by source inspection of pal/ linux_x86_64/net.hpp:305-312 plus full end-to-end functional proof (5000/5000 frames delivered correctly through a real cutover) rather than by a sanitizer catching the specific epoll_ctl failure path on Linux. Tie-breaking experiment: run the same c1c2c3_relay_recover scenario on a Linux CI leg with the epoll pal backend and assert io_.add_fd()'s return value is checked (or instrument epoll_ctl call counts) to directly witness the EEXIST-avoidance the fix provides.
  • Design 2's C1/C2/C3 proofs, and Design 3's, both ran on Windows/WSAPoll only — no TSan leg was available anywhere in this proof round (stated toolchain constraint). The ASan+UBSan (via clang, real sanitizer, not MSVC's ASan-only) plus reentrancy-assert plus cross-run-determinism combination is the strongest substitute obtained, consistent with VERIFICATION.md's documented Windows exclusions, but a genuine happens-before violation that never manifests as a memory error and is deterministic across ~20 runs would still be undetected. A Linux+TSan CI leg for this specific scenario (concurrent send() + set_relay() + fallback/recovery churn) is recommended follow-up.
  • DirectThenRelay<TimeoutMs>'s single timeout parameter double-duty: the same constant governs both the give-up threshold and, indirectly (via arm_direct_probe's re-arm-on-TimeoutMs cadence), the direct re-probe interval, with no backoff/jitter of its own on the probe retries. A permanently unreachable-but-not-SWIM-dead peer burns one extra tcp_connect attempt per TimeoutMs indefinitely. Acceptable at second-scale timeouts; a follow-on DirectThenRelay<TimeoutMs, ProbeIntervalMs = TimeoutMs> is a compatible future extension, not required now.
  • Relay-node health is out of scope by design (per this ADR's non-goals) and remains silently entangled: if the relay itself is unreachable while a peer is relay-routed, that peer's frames dead-end at the (also forever-retrying, now-durable-per-C3) relay Conn with no distinct signal beyond the existing drops_/reconnects_ counters. An operator cannot currently distinguish "relay is down" from "peer is down" from diagnostics alone.
  • Proactive abandonment of a still-possibly-succeeding Connecting attempt at the timeout deadline is a new way to trigger 010's existing at-most-once loss contract (today's forever-retry never gives up, so it never discards an attempt that might have completed a moment later). This is within the existing delivery-guarantee contract, not a new violation of it, but is a behavioral change worth naming in 017's text (see spec recommendations).
  • Design 1's per-peer chasing-watermark mechanism (C2r's own local invariant) was never falsified — only the end-to-end no-reordering property was. If a future round wants to revisit Design 1 (e.g. for its measured multi-peer contention advantages), the fix path is disclosed in the cross- examination record: route_hop must be re-consulted (or already-queued direct-hop entries must be migrated) at the instant relay_routed flips, not only at original enqueue time.

#Spec recommendations

  • 010-Distribution.md: Add a subsection documenting the direct↔relay endpoint-fallback policy as a TcpTransport-level, non-Transport-subclassing mechanism: NoRelayFallback (default) and DirectThenRelay<TimeoutMs>, resolved to a runtime int64_t at construction. State explicitly that relay routing changes which Endpoint a peer's Conn dials, never MessageFrame::to, outq_'s per-logical-peer keying, or the SWIM dead-letter contract on close_peer — the frame's addressing and per-peer FIFO ordering are untouched by the routing decision. Cross-reference this ADR for the proven fd-handoff (del_fd before add_fd on cutover) and dial-target-resolution (single resolve_dial_endpoint() call site shared by dial()/ensure_conn() and do_reconnect()) invariants any future relay-adjacent change must preserve.
  • 017-Delivery-Guarantees.md: Add an explicit statement that a relay-routed peer's FIFO ordering guarantee is preserved across a recovery-triggered cutover from relay back to direct — no reordering, no duplication — and name the mechanism class (a fenced cutover that never splices mid-frame, deferred until the in-flight relay-hop frame has fully left the wire) as the required shape for any implementation, since a naive "flip on next Open" implementation (Design 1's original approach) was proven to reorder. Also document that a proactive give-up (abandoning a still-Connecting direct attempt at a wall-clock deadline to redirect to relay) is a new, disclosed trigger of the existing at-most-once loss contract, not an exception to it.
  • 021-Cluster-Formation-and-Lifecycle.md: Note that relay-node Endpoint acquisition (static config today; SWIM capability-gossip piggyback per ADR-045 as a follow-on) and relay-node health/failover are explicitly deferred non-goals of the fallback-threshold policy decided here — cross-reference this ADR so a future relay-discovery ADR does not need to re-litigate the fallback-threshold mechanism itself, only how a peer's designated relay Endpoint is learned/ updated at runtime via the already-proven, loop-thread-marshaled set_relay().
  • 019-Platform-Abstraction-Layer.md: Record the concrete backend asymmetry this ADR's C1 fix depends on: IoContext::add_fd on the Linux/epoll backend fails (EEXIST, silently, return value discarded by a careless caller) when called on an fd already registered in that epoll instance, while the Windows/WSAPoll backend's add_fd unconditionally overwrites the stored handler and masks the same bug class. Either (a) document this as a caller obligation — always del_fd before re-add_fd-ing a live fd, as this ADR's cutover_to_direct now does — or (b) file a follow-on PAL hardening item to make add_fd idempotent/replace-semantics on both backends so the two pal implementations cannot silently diverge in behavior for the same caller mistake. Given 019's own parity contract ("unchanged between the Linux and Windows backends"), option (b) is preferable long term; this ADR does not implement it, only surfaces the asymmetry it uncovered.
